text: Lateral movement is simply this: using the access and credentials gained from one compromised host to reach additional hosts in the same environment. It's rarely a single dramatic technique. It's almost always the same valid credential or trust relationship being reused somewhere else it's also valid. That's exactly why it's detectable — legitimate authentication infrastructure already records every one of those events, whether it's a real admin logging into three servers in a row or something else.

A handful of detection signatures come up again and again. The same account authenticating to many different hosts within a short window. Authentication coming from an unexpected source, like a service account that suddenly shows up on a workstation instead of its usual application server. A privileged account logging in somewhere it's never used before. And a spike of failed authentications immediately followed by a success, across multiple hosts — a classic signature whether it comes from credential guessing or a replayed credential.

Sentinel's sign-in and authentication tables, covered back in course 6, are built specifically to surface these patterns. A single user account hitting five servers in a few minutes is unusual for almost any real job function, and that's exactly the kind of baseline deviation a correlation rule is written to catch — tying the KQL detection content from earlier in this path directly into what you're learning here.

Here's the pattern underneath nearly every one of these signatures: an identical, reusable credential crossed a boundary it shouldn't have. That's why credential hygiene matters as much as detection does. Course 8's identity engineering content — unique local administrator passwords, credential tiering, Privileged Access Workstations — and this course's own microsegmentation content from chapter 3 both work toward the same goal: leaving nothing reusable for a compromised credential to move with.

That's the real takeaway: the best lateral-movement finding on an authorized engagement is proof that a credential's reach extends further than it should — and the best defense isn't a cleverer detection rule, it's removing the reusable credential in the first place. Next lesson shifts from detection and defense to the professional obligation that closes out every engagement: documenting and removing anything you created during an authorized test.
